request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: Caucasian woman with insulin-dependent diabetes and hypertension
Age: 51 years

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient was admitted with a perimesencephalic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in the prepontine, interpeduncular, ambient, and crural cisterns. She had a previous SAH due to a 6mm aneurysm in the anterior communicating artery (Acomm), which was treated with endovascular coiling.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient's hospital course was complicated by vasospasm and cerebral salt wasting. She was treated with hypervolemia, hypertension, intra-arterial nicardipine, and sodium and volume supplementation. After discharge, she returned to work with no residual neurologic deficits.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
N/A

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient had a follow-up magnetic resonance imaging and angiography performed six months later, which demonstrated no vascular abnormalities.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:
The patient was discharged home in good condition on post-bleed day 10.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The patient was admitted with a perimesencephalic subarachnoid hemorrhage. In ICD-10, nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is I60 (Subarachnoid haemorrhage). The summary notes a prior aneurysm that was coiled, but this admission's bleed is perimesencephalic and non-aneurysmal, with follow-up angiography showing no vascular abnormality. Because the bleed was not caused by a ruptured aneurysm, I60 is chosen over I67 (other cerebrovascular diseases).

The I60 subcategories are:
- I60.0 to I60.6 cover hemorrhage from specified arteries.
- I60.7 covers an unspecified intracranial artery.
- I60.8 covers other subarachnoid hemorrhage.
- I60.9 covers unspecified.

Perimesencephalic hemorrhage would most likely be I60.8, but the question asks only for the three-character category.

Vasospasm and cerebral salt wasting are complications of the hemorrhage, so they are secondary diagnoses and do not change the principal diagnosis.

CODE: I60
